period_summary: Citations are heavily concentrated in the 2nd–4th centuries, reflecting the verse's central role in Christological debates about divine sonship and the nature of Christ's relationship to the Father.

citations.cited_text: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee
citations.text_form_note: The citation matches the LXX rendering 'υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε' exactly, including the demonstrative pronoun σύ (you) characteristic of the Greek tradition.
citations.theological_use: Justin employs this verse as a proof-text for Christ's divine sonship, arguing against Trypho that the 'begetting' refers to Christ's incarnation or resurrection, not adoptionism. It demonstrates Christ's unique relationship to the Father.
citations.transmission_implication: Confirms that the Greek LXX text form was standard in mid-2nd century Christian apologetic contexts in Rome.

citations.cited_text: Thou art my Son; today I have begotten thee
citations.text_form_note: The citation reflects the LXX word order and vocabulary, transmitted through either direct Greek reading or Latin translation of the LXX tradition (Vetus Latina).
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses this text to refute Gnostic claims, insisting that the 'begetting' refers to the eternal generation of the Son and is manifested in the incarnation. It supports orthodox Christology against docetic interpretations.
citations.transmission_implication: Shows LXX-based text circulation in Gaul by the late 2nd century, likely mediated through Old Latin translations.

citations.cited_text: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Latin citation follows the Vetus Latina tradition derived from the LXX, using 'hodie' (today) which translates σήμερον, the key temporal indicator in the Greek text.
citations.theological_use: Tertullian deploys this verse against Modalistic Monarchianism (Praxeas), arguing for the real distinction between Father and Son while maintaining unity of substance. The 'begetting' indicates the Son's procession from the Father.
citations.transmission_implication: Demonstrates that North African Latin Christianity relied on LXX-based Old Latin versions in the early 3rd century.

citations.cited_text: υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
citations.text_form_note: Origen preserves the full LXX text with precision, including all Greek particles. His Hexapla work indicates awareness of Hebrew and other versions, but he consistently cites the LXX form in theological works.
citations.theological_use: Origen interprets 'today' as signifying the eternal generation of the Son—a timeless 'today' that is always present. This becomes foundational for later patristic theology of eternal sonship, countering temporal or adoptionist readings.
citations.transmission_implication: Confirms the LXX as the authoritative text form in Alexandrian scholarly Christianity, even among those with knowledge of the Hebrew.

citations.cited_text: υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὰ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius quotes the standard LXX form verbatim, showing no influence from Hebrew or other textual traditions. His citation is consistent across multiple works.
citations.theological_use: Critical for Athanasius's anti-Arian polemic: he argues that 'begotten' (γεγέννηκά) demonstrates the Son's consubstantiality with the Father against Arian claims of creaturehood. The verse proves eternal, not temporal, generation.
citations.transmission_implication: Demonstrates the stability and dominance of the LXX text form in 4th-century Alexandrian orthodoxy during the Arian controversy.

citations.cited_text: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
citations.text_form_note: Hilary's Latin follows the established Vetus Latina rendering from the LXX, maintaining 'hodie' as the critical temporal marker that he interprets as eternal present.
citations.theological_use: Hilary uses this verse extensively in his Trinitarian theology to defend Nicene orthodoxy in the West. He interprets 'today' as the eternal generation of the Son, emphasizing that divine begetting transcends temporal categories.
citations.transmission_implication: Shows continuity of LXX-based Latin text tradition in Western theological discourse through the mid-4th century Trinitarian debates.

citations.cited_text: υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
citations.text_form_note: Basil reproduces the LXX text with complete fidelity, showing no textual variation or influence from Hexaplaric recensions despite his Cappadocian scholarly context.
citations.theological_use: Basil employs the verse against Eunomius to argue for the Son's full divinity and eternal generation. He emphasizes that 'begotten' distinguishes the Son's mode of being from the Father's without implying subordination or temporal origin.
citations.transmission_implication: Confirms that even in scholarly Cappadocian circles with access to multiple text forms, the standard LXX remained the authoritative citation base.

citations.cited_text: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
citations.text_form_note: Augustine cites the Old Latin version derived from the LXX throughout his psalm commentary, though he occasionally references Jerome's Psalterium iuxta Hebraeos for comparative purposes without adopting its readings.
citations.theological_use: Augustine offers multiple interpretations: eternal generation of the Son, the incarnation, and the resurrection. He sees 'today' as referring to both timeless eternity and historical moments of revelation, integrating the verse into his broader theology of divine immutability.
citations.transmission_implication: Shows the persistence of LXX-based Latin texts in North African exegesis into the early 5th century, even after Jerome's Hebrew-based translations became available.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation evidence for Psalm 2:7 reveals unanimous reliance on the LXX text form across all geographical regions and throughout the entire period surveyed (2nd–5th centuries). No citations show influence from the proto-MT Hebrew tradition, mixed readings, or independent text forms. This remarkable uniformity indicates that the Greek LXX was the exclusive scriptural authority for Christian theological discourse on this passage, even among fathers who had knowledge of Hebrew (like Origen) or access to Jerome's Hebraica veritas translations (like Augustine). The stability of the citation formula 'υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε' across Greek-speaking regions and its consistent Latin equivalent 'Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te' in the West demonstrates a controlled textual transmission through established ecclesial reading traditions rather than ad hoc translation practices.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers from the 2nd through 5th centuries all quoted Psalm 2:7 from the Greek Septuagint translation, not from the Hebrew text. This Greek version became the standard Bible for Christian theology, especially in debates about who Jesus was and his relationship to God the Father. The text remained remarkably stable across different regions and centuries.

notable_variants.reading: υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε (You are my Son; today I have begotten you)
notable_variants.significance: This is the standard LXX reading attested universally in patristic sources. The word σήμερον ('today') became theologically crucial in debates about eternal generation versus temporal adoption, with orthodox fathers interpreting it as an eternal present rather than a historical moment.

notable_variants.reading: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te
notable_variants.significance: This Old Latin rendering, directly based on the LXX, became the standard Western citation form. The retention of 'hodie' (today) from σήμερον was theologically significant in Western Trinitarian theology, particularly for Hilary and Augustine's doctrines of eternal generation.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Uniform LXX Transmission in Christological Controversy Context
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The complete absence of proto-MT or mixed citations for Psalm 2:7 in patristic sources is striking and reveals that the LXX functioned as a closed textual tradition for this theologically critical passage. Despite awareness of Hebrew texts among some fathers and the availability of Jerome's Hebraica translations by the late 4th century, no father appealed to alternative text forms even when defending contested Christological positions. This suggests that the LXX text was not merely a translation convenience but held authoritative scriptural status that transcended linguistic or text-critical considerations.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: All early Christian writers quoted this verse from the Greek translation, never from Hebrew, showing that the Greek Bible had become Christianity's authoritative Scripture. Even scholars who knew Hebrew stuck with the Greek version for theological arguments.

_validation.confidence_note: The overall thesis (LXX-dominant transmission of Ps 2:7 in patristic sources) is sound and well-established, but several specific citation references contain inaccuracies and one citation has a textual error.

flagged_claims.claim: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, ch. 88
flagged_claims.reason: Justin cites Ps 2:7 most prominently in Dialogue 88 in connection with Jesus' baptism, but the citation there reflects a Lukan/Western variant ('Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee' applied to the baptism via Luke 3:22 D). The note claims it 'matches the LXX exactly,' but Justin's interest here is the baptismal voice, and the context blurs Ps 2:7 with the Synoptic baptism narrative—worth verifying the exact chapter and form.

The specific reference III.19.2 for Ps 2:7 should be verified; Irenaeus discusses Christ's sonship in this region but the precise citation locus needs checking. Also, the theological gloss attributing 'eternal generation' language to Irenaeus is anachronistic—that doctrine is properly Origenian.

flagged_claims.claim: Tertullian, Against Praxeas, ch. 11, 'Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te'
flagged_claims.reason: Tertullian does cite Ps 2:7 in Adv. Praxean (ch. 7 and elsewhere), but ch. 11 as the locus should be verified. The exact Latin wording attributed may also reflect a modernized form rather than Tertullian's actual citation.

flagged_claims.claim: Athanasius citation 'υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὰ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε'
flagged_claims.reason: The Greek text contains an error: 'ἐγὰ' is not a Greek word; it should be 'ἐγὼ'. This is presented as a verbatim citation with high confidence (0.88), undermining the claim of fidelity.

flagged_claims.claim: Basil of Caesarea, Against Eunomius, II.12
flagged_claims.reason: The specific section II.12 for Ps 2:7 needs verification; Basil discusses generation extensively in Adv. Eunomium but the precise citation locus is not confirmable without checking.

flagged_claims.claim: Hilary of Poitiers, De Trinitate, XII.36
flagged_claims.reason: Hilary cites Ps 2:7 multiple times in De Trinitate (notably Books IV, VI, XII), but XII.36 specifically should be verified. The reference appears plausible but is not independently confirmed.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen interprets 'today' as signifying the eternal generation of the Son—a timeless 'today'
flagged_claims.reason: While the 'eternal today' interpretation is associated with Origen broadly, the specific locus De Principiis I.2.4 should be checked; this interpretation is more clearly developed in his Commentary on Romans and Hom. on Jeremiah than necessarily in De Princ. I.2.4.

flagged_claims.claim: Augustine 'occasionally references Jerome's Psalterium iuxta Hebraeos for comparative purposes without adopting its readings'
flagged_claims.reason: Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos generally uses Old Latin/Gallican-type texts, but the specific claim about his comparative use of Jerome's iuxta Hebraeos for Ps 2 is an over-precise generalization.

flagged_claims.claim: transmission_implication for Irenaeus: 'likely mediated through Old Latin translations'
flagged_claims.reason: Irenaeus wrote in Greek; Adv. Haereses survives primarily in Latin translation. The claim that his citation was 'mediated through Old Latin' confuses the transmission of the work with Irenaeus's own source text, which would have been Greek LXX.

safe_claims: The LXX form 'υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε' is the standard Greek reading of Ps 2:7
Patristic citations of Ps 2:7 overwhelmingly follow the LXX rather than a proto-MT form
The verse was central to Christological debates about divine sonship
'Hodie' in Old Latin renders σήμερον from the LXX
Athanasius used Ps 2:7 in anti-Arian polemic regarding the Son's generation
Justin Martyr cites Ps 2:7 in Dialogue with Trypho in connection with Christ's sonship
